body.text: After a six-year hiatus, the China-India border trade via Shipki Pass, a 3,930-meter pass in Himachal Pradesh’s Kinnaur district, resumed on August 1, 2026. After the 2020 Galwan military standoff, the border trade from this pass, often called the “Gateway to Tibet,” was suspended. With limited operations and economic scope but significant political symbolism, the resumption of border trade has also rejuvenated interest in the competing legitimacy narratives over the Tibet question.

According to China’s state-affiliated think tanks and media, border trade via the Shipki L Pass dates to the 7th to 9th centuries when the Tubo Empire reigned over the plateau. China frames trade along this route as a sub-set of the Silk Road. Between the 14th and early 20th centuries, Chinese tellings claim Tibet as a commercial bridge between China and South Asia, while in the late 18th century, the Qing Dynasty of China took measures to standardize trade activities between Tibet and its neighboring countries, for “better management” of Tibet.

As per the Chinese accounts, the “peaceful liberation” of Tibet in 1951 and the signing of the Panchsheel Pact led to the abolishment of India’s trade “privileges” in Tibet and the formalization of a new paradigm for Indo-Tibetan trade.

China claims to have set Sino-Indian border trade free from unequal terms set by colonial rule, ushering in an era of normalized development. Cut to the present: the reopening of Shipki La Pass, despite the minuscule trade volume, is received by Chinese media as a welcome move toward improving China-India strategic ties.
Every aspect of the Chinese reading of history sidelines the Tibetan side of the story. For starters, what the Chinese narrative misses is the independent agency Tibet exercised before 1951.

By contrast, Tibetan scholars characterize Shipki Pass as a major route for trade and cultural exchange between Indian territories and Tibet, independent of Chinese involvement. Consistent with Tibet’s claim to political and commercial autonomy, historical records describe Shipki Pass as a crucial route connecting Tibet with the Kingdom of Bushahar, Ladakh, and Kashmir. The exchange across the regions, involving a variety of products, was governed by gamgya, a traditional informal oath of mutual trust that was respected and maintained across generations.

However, with the development of modern state infrastructure on either side of Shipki Pass and growing geopolitical disputes culminating in the Sino-Indian War in 1962, the centuries-old trade system was fractured.

The Tibetan accounts also challenge the Chinese manipulation of history to appropriate the Shipki Pass trade route into a meta-narrative of the Silk Road. The commentaries consistent with the Tibetan narrative challenge the engulfing of Tibet in Chinese historical narratives as a simple commercial bridge, stripping it of its agency and independent existence.

Tibetan scholars argue that it was the PRC’s administrative and military consolidation post 1951 that led to the dismantling of traditional trade and transit networks, not the British colonial disruption. The PRC’s normalization with India involved the isolation of Tibet and the enforcement of new restrictions on previously autonomous trade practices between India and Tibet
This is not a dispute over mere historical fact-checking. It leads to the question of who holds legitimacy over Tibet, and the framing of the India-China-Tibet relationship since the 1950s.

The re-opening of Shipki Pass – often framed in terms of the overall China-India relationship – is seeing one version of history eclipse the other. Popular media crowds out the complicated, contesting narratives and historical claims by constructing a more attractive narrative around boosting local trade, development, and restoration of ancient ties. Given the meager economic value of this barter-driven border trade, the Chinese media has woven the narrative around regional livelihood, the possibility of infrastructure development, and building mutual trust. The Chinese commentary construes the opening as a “revival” of ancient Sino-Indian border trade, with Tibet as a commercial bridge, and part of efforts to eliminate the colonial inequalities after the “liberation of Tibet.”

Over the last few years, the construction of border village resettlement projects, combining civilian housing with military and surveillance infrastructure, in the Tibet Autonomous Region near the Shipki Pass has gained momentum. These villages help give physical form to China’s version of the story, elevating ancient Sino-Indian trade ties over India-Tibet exchanges. Expanding beyond academic and journalistic narratives, Beijing is consolidating its rendition of Tibet as a commercial bridge through trade resumption and border infrastructure.

The reopening of Shipki Pass matters for reasons beyond trade resumption and China-India diplomacy. It highlights the disputes over sovereignty, history, and measures to consolidate control over the border. As it turns out, the trade diplomacy along the Sino-Indian border is less about trade and more about whose history triumphs.
